nameStory: The Green Wood Cup gets its charming name from its tiny, saucer-shaped fruiting bodies that look like miniature green teacups nestled in decaying wood. The 'green' part is especially fitting since this fungus is famous for turning wood a brilliant blue-green color, creating natural artwork in the forest.
description: The Green Wood Cup is a small saprophytic fungus that feeds on dead hardwood, breaking it down as nature's recycler. While the actual cup-shaped fruiting bodies are quite rare to spot, this fungus is much more commonly recognized by the stunning blue-green staining it creates in rotting wood. The cups themselves are tiny and saucer-shaped when they do appear, but most people encounter this species through its signature colored wood rather than the mushrooms.

idTips.label: Blue-green wood staining
idTips.description: Look for wood that has been stained a striking turquoise or blue-green color, almost like it's been painted with watercolors. The stained wood feels normal to touch but the color penetrates deep into the grain.

idTips.label: Cup-shaped fruiting bodies
idTips.description: When present, the actual mushrooms are tiny green saucers or shallow cups, smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch, typically less than half an inch across.

idTips.label: Hardwood substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on decaying hardwood logs and branches, particularly oak, maple, and beech. The wood is usually soft and punky, easily crumbling when pressed.

idTips.label: Scattered distribution
idTips.description: The green staining appears in patches or streaks through the wood grain rather than covering entire surfaces uniformly.

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly in areas with abundant fallen hardwood logs and branches. Look for it in moist, shaded woodland areas where dead oak, maple, beech, and other hardwoods are slowly decomposing on the forest floor.

seasonality.spring: Green-stained wood becomes more visible as snow melts and forest debris is exposed. The vivid coloring stands out against brown leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding the blue-green stained wood as moisture levels support active fungal growth. Actual cup fruiting bodies are most likely to appear during humid summer months.
seasonality.fall: Continued opportunity to spot stained wood, though new leaf fall may obscure some specimens. Fresh windfall may reveal newly colonized wood.
seasonality.winter: Green-stained wood remains visible and identifiable under snow cover, though actual fruiting bodies are absent during cold months.

funFact: This fungus creates wood so beautifully colored that it's been harvested for centuries to make 'tunbridge ware' - intricate wooden inlay work prized by furniture makers and craftspeople, turning a simple forest decomposer into a source of natural art supplies!
confusionNotes: The blue-green stained wood is quite distinctive and rarely confused with anything else in nature. However, don't confuse it with copper-stained wood around old buildings or treated lumber, which has a more metallic, artificial-looking green color and lacks the natural grain penetration.
contextualKnowledge: Many people encounter the beautiful green-stained wood long before they learn about the tiny fungus responsible for creating it. The wood staining is actually the fungus living inside the wood fibers, not just growing on the surface, which is why the color goes so deep into the grain.
compareHints: Green Wood Cup is very similar to its close relative the Turquoise Elfcup, and the two are often difficult to distinguish in the field. Both create nearly identical blue-green wood staining, but Turquoise Elfcup tends to be slightly more common and may have subtly different spore characteristics visible only under microscopic examination.
